summary: Nizatidine is a histamine H2-receptor antagonist that decreases gastric acid secretion. It is used to treat and prevent duodenal and gastric ulcers, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), and erosive esophagitis. It is well tolerated, with headache being the most common adverse effect. Unlike cimetidine, it has little effect on cytochrome P450 and minimal antiandrogenic activity. Dose reduction is required in patients with renal impairment because the drug is primarily eliminated renally.

moa: Nizatidine competitively and reversibly binds to histamine H2 receptors located on the basolateral membrane of gastric parietal cells. By blocking histamine-mediated stimulation, it reduces both basal (including nocturnal) and food-, caffeine-, betazole-, and pentagastrin-stimulated gastric acid secretion, lowering acid output and concentration. This promotes healing of acid-related mucosal injury and relieves symptoms of acid reflux and ulcer disease.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to nizatidine or other H2-receptor antagonists
relative: Symptomatic response does not exclude gastric malignancy
monitor: Liver enzymes if hepatic dysfunction suspected

preg: Limited human data. Animal studies at high doses did not show clear teratogenicity. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus.
lact: Nizatidine is secreted into human breast milk in proportion to plasma concentration (approximately 0.1% of an oral dose). Because of potential for adverse effects in the nursing infant, use with caution or consider not breastfeeding.
renal: Nizatidine is eliminated primarily by the kidney; clearance falls and half-life rises with declining renal function. Reduce dose and/or lengthen the dosing interval in patients with moderate to severe renal impairment based on creatinine clearance.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is recommended for hepatic impairment. Rare reversible hepatic enzyme elevations and, very rarely, hepatocellular or cholestatic injury have been reported; discontinue if hepatitis develops.

moderate: High-dose aspirin (e.g., 3900 mg/day) - nizatidine may raise serum salicylate levels
Drugs whose absorption is pH-dependent (e.g., ketoconazole, itraconazole, atazanavir) - reduced absorption due to higher gastric pH
minor: Minimal effect on cytochrome P450; clinically significant CYP interactions are uncommon
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; tomato-based foods/juices may interact with some product matrices but are not clinically significant.
interactions.alcohol: Alcohol can raise gastric acid and irritate the mucosa; limit intake. Some reports suggest H2 blockers may modestly increase blood alcohol.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause false-positive urobilinogen tests with Multistix; can affect gastric acid secretion studies.

missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose. Do not take two doses at once.
overdose: Overdose experience is limited; expected effects relate to exaggerated pharmacology (e.g., cholinergic-type signs in animals). If overdose occurs, remove unabsorbed drug, observe, and provide supportive and symptomatic care. Hemodialysis removes little drug. Contact a poison control center.
